# Tidal Locking and Its Profound Influence on Planetary Climates

Tidal locking occurs when a planet's rotation period matches its orbital period, causing one hemisphere to face its star permanently. This phenomenon, common among planets orbiting red dwarf stars, creates some of the most extreme and fascinating climates in the universe.

The most obvious consequence is the dramatic temperature contrast between hemispheres. The dayside, bathed in perpetual starlight, can reach temperatures hot enough to vaporize rock on close-orbiting worlds, while the nightside plunges to frigid depths where atmospheres themselves may freeze out. On planets like the real exoplanet LHS 3844b, models suggest dayside temperatures exceeding 800 Kelvin.

However, tidal locking doesn't necessarily doom a planet to climatic extremes. If a planet retains a substantial atmosphere, winds redistribute heat from dayside to nightside. Climate models of tidally locked worlds show that a dense enough atmosphere—perhaps 1 bar or more—can moderate temperatures sufficiently to maintain liquid water across much of the surface. These atmospheric currents, combined with ocean circulation on water worlds, could create a temperate ring called the terminator zone, where permanent twilight offers potentially habitable conditions.

The climate dynamics also produce unique weather patterns. Simulations predict permanent cloud formation on the dayside, which reflects starlight and cools the surface. Some models show a persistent eye-shaped storm or cloud cluster at the substellar point, analogous to Jupiter
